newsitem.title: USA: Airport wars escalate between Chicago and Illinois.
newsitem.headline: Airport wars escalate between Chicago and Illinois.

text.p: It's a multi-year, multi-layered legal battle that pits Republican state of Illinois officials against the Democratic minions of Mayor Richard Daley's Chicago.
And so far, nobody's winning, except maybe the lawyers.

The latest skirmish has been over a small airport on Chicago's downtown lakefront. Daley and his hand-picked Chicago Park District administration want to close Meigs Field on Sept. 30 and build a $27 million, bond-financed nature park.

Gov. Jim Edgar, a regular user of the airport with his state plane, wants to keep it open, contending the facility, which is mainly used by corporate jets and private plane owners, is an essential tool for the city and state economy.

Last Wednesday, the Chicago City Council voted in favour of the park plan, triggering the filing Thursday of a petition in the Illinois Supreme Court by the state seeking to block the city's planned demolition of the airport and authorise the Illinois Department of Transportation to take it over.
The state also joined a lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court by a group of pilots and plane owners seeking to keep the airport open.

In addition, Illinois filed suit in Cook County Circuit Court charging that Chicago breached its contract with the state that requires the city to operate Meigs Field for 20 years after the receipt of state improvement grants for the facility or until the useful life of those improvements has ended.
"We're trying to stop the city from shooting itself in the economic foot," said Gary Mack, Edgar's spokesman.
For its part, Chicago called the lawsuits "a waste of taxpayers money."

"The fact that the state filed three separate lawsuits in three different forums on the same subject reflects desperation rather than confidence," said city corporation counsel Susan Sher in a statement.
The battle over Meigs Field is just the latest in a number of pending legal actions involving Chicago airports.

The root of the wars can be traced to the failure of a Daley and Edgar-supported plan to build a $10.8 billion, largely bond-financed airport on the city's southeast side. The plan, which resulted from prodding of federal aviation officials looking to relieve air congestion in the Chicago region, died a quick death in the Illinois General Assembly in 1992.
Later that year, Edgar proposed building an airport in Peotone, a town 35 miles southwest of Chicago.

But Daley had given up on the idea of a new Chicago-area airport and vowed to spend money to improve the city's existing O'Hare International and Midway airports, much to the fright of suburbs near O'Hare that don't want to see an additional runway built there. Daley flatly refused to support the governor's airport plan.
Still, the spector of the $2.3 billion airport in Peotone planted fears in Chicago that the state would move to siphon city airport funds to help build that facility.

Indeed, lawmakers in the Republican-controlled General Assembly introduced a bill last year seeking to create a state-dominated regional airport authority that would own and control Chicago's airports, as well as build the Peotone facility.
That move was met with the expeditious signing of a bi-state regional airport authority pact between Chicago and Gary, Ind. with the thought there was only room for one regional airport authority.
With the battle lines now crossing state lines, Edgar shot back with a lawsuit in U.S. District Court seeking to nullify the bi-state agreement.
